name: Automated decision-making disclosure laws (United States)
blurb: Four US instruments that regulate automated or algorithmic decisions about people. They differ on which decisions they reach, who must comply, and what the core duty is.

cells.5: Use of automated decision-making technology for “significant decisions” about consumers, under the CCPA framework.
cells.15: Automated decision-making that produces a consequential decision about a Colorado resident.
cells.18: Predictive data analytics in employment; amends the Human Rights Act and the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act.
cells.19: Automated employment decision tools used to screen NYC job candidates or employees.

cells.5: Point-of-collection notice, an opt-out toggle that honors Global Privacy Control, and a right to access the decision logic.
cells.15: Disclosure to the affected person that an automated system was used in a consequential decision.
cells.18: Bars discrimination through predictive analytics and reaches deceptive-practice claims; disclosure and anti-bias duties on employers.
cells.19: An independent bias audit within the prior year, published results, and advance notice to candidates.

cells.5: Enforced by the California Privacy Protection Agency; obligations phase in on a schedule set in the rules.
cells.15: Enforcement paused pending xAI v. Weiser. The Act repeals the earlier SB 24-205.
cells.18: Enforced through the Illinois Human Rights Act mechanism.
cells.19: Enforced by the NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection; civil penalties per violation.

name: Frontier-model safety and transparency regimes
blurb: Four regimes aimed at the largest, most capable AI models. They converge on published safety frameworks and incident reporting, and differ on the threshold that pulls a model in and on how hard the obligation bites.

cells.17: Frontier developers above a large training-compute threshold.
cells.23: Frontier models, on thresholds aligned to California SB 53.
cells.28: “High-performance” AI, with a statutory threshold of 10^26 training FLOPs.
cells.2: “Covered frontier models” as defined by the order.

cells.17: Publish a frontier AI safety framework and report critical safety incidents.
cells.23: Adopt and disclose a safety and security protocol; report incidents. Creates a dedicated NYDFS oversight office.
cells.28: Risk management and transparency duties; large foreign providers above revenue or user thresholds must appoint a domestic representative.
cells.2: A voluntary 30-day pre-release review window for covered models, plus a Treasury-led AI Cybersecurity Clearinghouse.

cells.17: Statute in force; civil penalties available to the California Attorney General.
cells.23: Enacted, effective 1 January 2027; enforcement through the NY Attorney General and NYDFS.
cells.28: In force with a one-year grace period on penalties; enforced by the Ministry of Science and ICT.
cells.2: Executive order, voluntary. No direct penalty; drives federal coordination and procurement expectations.

name: Voluntary AI risk and security frameworks
blurb: The four non-binding references the field treats as the baseline. Two are US government risk frameworks, one is a certifiable international management standard, one is an application-security checklist.

cells.3: The full AI lifecycle, any AI system.
cells.4: Generative AI specifically — a companion profile to the AI RMF.
cells.11: Security of applications built on large language models.

cells.3: The Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions, plus a companion Playbook of suggested actions.
cells.4: Twelve generative-AI risk vectors — confabulation, data privacy, supply-chain integrity and others — mapped to AI RMF actions.
cells.29: Auditable requirements for setting up, running, and improving an AI management system.
cells.11: The ten critical LLM-application risks, including prompt injection, insecure output handling, and excessive agency.

name: Generative-AI transparency and disclosure rules
blurb: Four rules governing what a generative or conversational AI system must tell the people it interacts with, and what it must reveal about how it was built.

cells.8: Chatbots, generative and biometric systems whose outputs reach the EU.
cells.6: Generative AI systems made available to Californians, for models trained since January 2022.
cells.25: Public-facing generative AI services offered in mainland China.
cells.16: Consumer-facing chatbots available to Colorado users, with added duties where minors may be involved.

cells.8: Tell users they are interacting with AI, label deepfakes, and mark synthetic content in a machine-readable way.
cells.6: Publish a 12-point summary of the training datasets used, with no trade-secret exemption.
cells.25: Label AI-generated content and register the service; content and training data must meet CAC content rules.
cells.16: Disclose that the user is talking to AI, run age estimation, and follow self-harm response protocols.

cells.8: In force, phased; extraterritorial — applies wherever the output reaches an EU user. Fines up to €15M or 3% of global turnover.
cells.6: In force since 1 January 2026; enforced by the California Attorney General.
cells.25: In force since 15 August 2023; enforced by the Cyberspace Administration of China.
